articleHeader.title: Python Scope — The LEGB Rule Explained Properly
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you actually need to know about variable scope in Python — Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in resolution order, the global and nonlocal keywords, closures, and the exact UnboundLocalError you'll hit while learning this.

blocks.text: Scope answers one specific question: when your code says a name like total, which actual variable does Python mean? The same name can exist in several completely separate places at once — a total inside one function, a different total inside another, and a third total sitting at the top level of your script — and scope is the set of rules Python follows to figure out, for any given line of code, exactly which one you're talking about.

Python resolves this using a specific, ordered search called the LEGB rule — Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. When your code references a name, Python checks these four scopes in that exact order and uses the first match it finds. It's not a vague heuristic; it's a precise, deterministic algorithm that runs every single time a name is looked up, and once you actually know the order, a huge number of 'why isn't my variable updating' bugs stop being mysterious.

Here's the specific moment scope stopped being abstract for me: I had a function that read if count > threshold: where count was meant to be a variable the function itself incremented on every call, tracking state across multiple calls. It never worked — count stayed at zero forever, no matter how many times I called the function. The bug wasn't in the logic. It was that count += 1 inside the function silently created a brand-new local variable named count, completely separate from the global one I thought I was updating, and Python never told me this was happening — it just quietly did it, exactly per the LEGB rule, and I hadn't yet learned the rule well enough to see it coming.

This guide walks through all four LEGB scopes precisely, the global and nonlocal keywords that let you deliberately reach outside a function's local scope, how closures capture enclosing-scope variables, and the exact UnboundLocalError traceback that's almost always the direct symptom of a scope misunderstanding.

sections.title: History — How Python's Scoping Rules Evolved

blocks.text: Python's scoping model has genuinely changed shape over the decades, not just gained new keywords — an important thing to know if you ever read code or documentation written for an earlier version.

items.text: — Basic local and global scope existed from Python's earliest release, along with the global keyword, letting a function explicitly declare it intends to modify a module-level variable rather than create a new local one.

— In Python's earliest versions, nested functions could NOT read variables from an enclosing function's local scope at all — only from local and global/built-in scopes. A function defined inside another function was, for scoping purposes, almost as isolated as a top-level function.

— Introduced genuine nested scopes, formally adding the 'E' (Enclosing) to what would eventually be called the LEGB rule. This single change is what made real closures possible in Python, and it directly enabled the decorator pattern years before decorators had their own dedicated @ syntax.

— Introduced the nonlocal keyword, finally giving nested functions a clean, explicit way to MODIFY (not just read) a variable in an enclosing function's scope — something Python 2 genuinely had no clean syntax for at all, forcing awkward workarounds like wrapping a value in a mutable list.

— List comprehensions gained their own private scope in Python 3, meaning the loop variable inside a comprehension no longer leaks into the enclosing scope the way it did in Python 2 — a subtle but genuinely important scoping fix that eliminated a class of accidental variable-overwriting bugs.

— The LEGB rule, global, and nonlocal remain exactly as they've been since Python 3.0. This is one of the most stable areas of the language's core semantics, precisely because getting scoping rules right is foundational — changing them later would silently break enormous amounts of existing code.

blocks.text: Here are the 11 things worth knowing precisely about how Python scope actually behaves — not the loose version, the exact one:

items.title: LEGB Search Order
items.text: Python resolves a name by checking Local, then Enclosing, then Global, then Built-in scope, in that exact order, stopping at the first match found. This search happens for every single name lookup.

items.title: Functions Create Their Own Local Scope
items.text: Every function call gets a fresh, private local namespace. Variables assigned inside a function are local to that function by default and don't exist outside it.

items.title: Blocks Don't Create Scope
items.text: Unlike many languages, if, for, and while blocks in Python do NOT create their own scope. A variable assigned inside an if block or for loop is accessible after that block ends, within the same function or module.

items.title: Assignment Determines Locality
items.text: If a name is assigned anywhere inside a function body, Python treats it as local for the ENTIRE function — even on lines before that assignment. This is a compile-time decision, not a runtime one, and it's the root cause of most scope-related bugs.

items.title: global Declares Module-Level Intent
items.text: Writing global count inside a function tells Python that count refers to the module-level variable, not a new local one — allowing the function to genuinely modify the global value.

items.title: nonlocal Declares Enclosing-Function Intent
items.text: Writing nonlocal count inside a nested function tells Python that count refers to a variable in the nearest enclosing function's scope, not the module-level global or a new local — enabling genuine modification of that enclosing variable.

items.title: Reading Doesn't Require Declaration
items.text: You can freely READ a variable from an enclosing or global scope inside a function without any special keyword. global and nonlocal are only required when you intend to REASSIGN that name, not merely read it.

items.title: Closures Capture Enclosing Variables by Reference
items.text: A nested function that references an enclosing function's variable keeps access to that variable even after the enclosing function has finished executing — this is the mechanism behind Python closures and decorators.

items.title: Every Module Has Its Own Global Scope
items.text: Global scope is actually per-module, not truly program-wide. A variable defined at the top level of one .py file is that module's global scope, separate from another module's globals unless explicitly imported.

items.title: Built-in Scope Holds Python's Own Names
items.text: Names like len, print, range, and Exception live in the outermost Built-in scope, checked last — which is also why shadowing them (naming a variable list, for instance) silently hides the built-in within that scope.

items.title: Mutating vs Reassigning Are Scope-Different Operations
items.text: Calling a method that mutates a mutable object in place (like list.append()) doesn't require global or nonlocal, because you're not reassigning the name itself — only reassignment triggers Python's local-by-default rule.

sections.title: How Python Resolves a Variable Name — The LEGB Flowchart

blocks.text: Every single time your code references a variable name, Python runs through this exact search, in this exact order, checking one scope after another until it finds a match — or runs out of scopes and raises NameError.

nodes.label: 🪆 E — Enclosing Scope
nodes.sublabel: Any outer function this is nested in

blocks.text: Key insight: this search stops at the first match. If a variable named list exists locally inside your function, Python uses that local variable every time list is referenced in that function — it never even gets to Built-in scope to check Python's actual list type, silently shadowing it for the rest of that function's execution.

sections.title: How Scope Actually Works — Local-by-Default, global, and nonlocal

blocks.text: Three things separate someone who's memorised 'LEGB' as an acronym from someone who actually understands scope: knowing exactly when Python decides a variable is local, understanding precisely what global and nonlocal each do (and don't do), and recognising the specific traceback these misunderstandings produce.
✍️ The Rule That Trips Up Almost Everyone: Assignment Makes It Local

This is the single most important, most surprising rule in Python scoping: if a name is assigned anywhere inside a function's body, Python treats that name as local to the entire function — including on lines that come before the assignment. Python decides this at compile time, by scanning the whole function body for assignment statements, before the function ever actually runs. This is why count += 1 inside a function, intending to modify a module-level count, doesn't work as expected: count += 1 is really count = count + 1, which is an assignment, which makes Python treat count as local for that entire function — and then the read on the right-hand side (count, before the +) fails, because that local count hasn't been given a value yet at the point it's being read.
💥 UnboundLocalError — The Exact Error This Produces

Exactly this scenario raises UnboundLocalError: local variable 'count' referenced before assignment. This error message is precise and honest, but it confuses beginners because the variable clearly exists — just not the one they meant. Python correctly identifies count as local (because of the assignment somewhere in the function), and then correctly points out that this specific local variable has no value yet at the line where you're trying to read it. The fix isn't about the variable existing or not; it's about telling Python which scope you actually mean.
🌍 global — Reaching Out to Module-Level Scope

Adding global count as the first line inside the function tells Python explicitly: 'when this function uses the name count, it means the module-level variable, not a new local one.' With that declaration in place, count += 1 genuinely modifies the global value, and every subsequent call to the function sees the updated number. global must be declared before the variable is used in that function, and it applies only within that specific function's body — it doesn't leak into any other function.
🪆 nonlocal — Reaching Out to an Enclosing Function's Scope

nonlocal solves the identical problem one level down: a nested function that needs to modify a variable belonging to the function it's defined inside, rather than the module-level global or its own new local variable. This is exactly what a counter-generator closure pattern needs — an inner function incrementing a counter that lives in its enclosing function's scope, persisting across multiple calls to that inner function, without that counter ever touching module-level global scope at all.

Simple rule to remember: reading a variable from an outer scope needs no special keyword at all. Reassigning it does — global for module-level variables, nonlocal for enclosing-function variables. Mutating a mutable object in place (like my_list.append(x)) is a read of the reference plus a method call, not a reassignment, so it needs neither keyword.

blocks.text: Here's my honestly opinionated take: Python's decision to make if and for blocks NOT create their own scope is one of its more underrated design choices, and I say that as someone who's been genuinely bitten by it too. It means you don't need to pre-declare a variable above a loop just to use its final value after the loop ends, the way you sometimes do in block-scoped languages. The trade-off is that it makes the 'accidentally shadow the outer variable' mistake slightly easier to make inside functions — but honestly, that trade-off favours Python's broader goal of minimal ceremony over strict, block-by-block variable isolation.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Python's Scoping Model

blocks.text: Python's approach to scope is deliberately simple compared to many languages, and that simplicity has real costs alongside its real benefits.

pros.title: Simple, Predictable, Consistent Rule
pros.text: LEGB is one deterministic search order, applied identically everywhere in the language — no special cases for loops, conditionals, or try blocks to memorise separately.

pros.title: No Unnecessary Block-Level Ceremony
pros.text: Not needing block scope means you don't need to declare variables above a loop just to use their final value afterward — genuinely less boilerplate than block-scoped languages often require.

pros.title: Genuine, Fully-Working Closures
pros.text: Enclosing scope access, combined with nonlocal, gives Python real closures capable of both reading and modifying captured state — the foundation for decorators and factory functions.

pros.title: Explicit Intent for Outer-Scope Modification
pros.text: Requiring global and nonlocal for reassignment (though not for reading) forces a small, deliberate signal in the code whenever a function reaches outside its own local scope to change something.

pros.title: Encapsulation by Default
pros.text: Since every function gets its own private local namespace automatically, variables genuinely don't leak between unrelated functions unless you explicitly ask them to via global or nonlocal.

pros.title: Module-Level Global Scope Is Cleanly Isolated
pros.text: Because global scope is per-module rather than truly program-wide, importing modules doesn't silently pollute a shared global namespace the way some languages' global scope can.

cons.title: The Local-by-Default Assignment Rule Surprises Beginners
cons.text: That a single assignment anywhere in a function retroactively makes that name local for the WHOLE function, even before the assignment line, is genuinely counter-intuitive the first time it produces UnboundLocalError.

cons.title: Silent Shadowing of Built-ins
cons.text: Naming a local variable list, dict, or str silently hides Python's built-in of that name within that scope, with no warning — a subtle bug source, especially for beginners unaware they've done it.

cons.title: No Block Scope Can Cause Loop-Variable Leakage
cons.text: A variable assigned inside a for loop or if block remains accessible after that block ends, which occasionally causes confusion when a stale value from a previous iteration gets used unintentionally.

cons.title: Two Separate Keywords for a Similar Concept
cons.text: Needing both global and nonlocal, rather than one unified keyword, adds a bit of real cognitive overhead — remembering which one applies to which situation is a genuine, if small, learning cost.

cons.title: Late-Binding Closures Can Surprise
cons.text: Because closures capture enclosing variables by reference, not by value at creation time, functions created in a loop that reference the loop variable often behave unexpectedly, all sharing the same final value.

cons.title: Debugging Scope Issues Requires Understanding an Implicit Rule
cons.text: There's no visible syntax marking a variable as local versus outer-scope at the point of assignment — you have to know the local-by-default rule exists to correctly predict a function's behaviour just by reading it.

sections.title: Scope in Practice — From UnboundLocalError to Working global and nonlocal

blocks.text: Here's the exact broken version first, its precise error, and then the two correct fixes — one using global, one using nonlocal inside a closure.

blocks.label: broken_scope.py
lines: count += 1   # intends to modify the global count
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value

blocks.text: The fix, using global:
And the closure version, using nonlocal instead — a self-contained counter with no module-level global involved at all:
Practice This Code — Live Editor

blocks.initialCode:
x = 'global x'

def outer():
    x = 'enclosing x'
    def inner():
        print(x)
    inner()

outer()

blocks.text: Line-by-Line Explanation

items.html: count += 1 without global — Because count is assigned inside increment(), Python treats it as local for the whole function, and reading it on the right side of += before it has a local value raises UnboundLocalError.
global count — Declares, before any use, that count inside this function refers to the module-level variable. Now count += 1 correctly reads and writes that same global variable.
count = 0 inside make_counter() — This is increment()'s enclosing scope variable, not global — it belongs to make_counter()'s own local namespace.

nonlocal count inside increment() — Declares that this inner function's count refers to the enclosing function's count, not a new local one and not the module-level global (there isn't one here anyway).

counter_a and counter_b — Two separate calls to make_counter() create two entirely independent enclosing scopes, each with its own private count — which is exactly why calling counter_b() starts back at 1, unaffected by counter_a's calls.

sections.title: Where Scope Understanding Actually Matters — Real-World Applications

blocks.text: This isn't abstract theory — scope rules shape how real, working Python code is actually structured across many domains:

items.text: — Nearly every decorator relies on a nested function closing over variables from its enclosing function, exactly the Enclosing scope mechanism covered here — understanding LEGB is a genuine prerequisite for writing decorators confidently rather than by rote imitation.

— Functions that return other functions, each configured differently (like make_counter() above, or a make_multiplier(factor) that returns a function multiplying by that specific factor), depend entirely on closures capturing enclosing-scope state correctly.

Global-scope constants and configuration values (API_URL = '...', DEBUG = False) are extremely common at the top of real Python modules, and understanding exactly when a function needs global to modify them (versus just reading them, which needs nothing special) is a genuinely everyday skill.

items.strong: 🧵 Thread-Safe State and Avoiding Shared Mutable Globals
items.text: — Recognising that module-level global variables are shared across every part of a program that imports that module is exactly what motivates safer patterns like passing state explicitly as function arguments instead, especially in multi-threaded code.

— pytest fixtures and monkeypatching frequently rely on precise understanding of scope to correctly override or restore global and module-level state during tests without leaking changes between test cases.

items.strong: 🖥️ GUI Callback and Event Handler Design
items.text: — GUI frameworks often need callback functions defined inside a class or setup function that need to modify state defined in an enclosing scope — exactly the nonlocal use case, common in Tkinter-based applications.

— An enormous share of real-world Python debugging sessions, especially for less experienced developers, end up tracing back to exactly this: a function silently creating a new local variable instead of modifying the outer one the developer intended.

— Understanding that global scope is per-module, not program-wide, is essential for designing multi-file Python projects where different modules need their own independent top-level state without stepping on each other.

sections.title: Why Scope Deserves Real, Deliberate Study

blocks.text: Scope is one of those topics that seems simple in a two-paragraph tutorial summary and then quietly causes real, recurring confusion in actual code. Here's why it's worth the deeper look:

items.strong: 🐛 It's a Genuinely Common Source of Silent Bugs
items.text: — Unlike a syntax error, a scope mistake often doesn't crash — it just quietly produces the wrong result, like a counter that never actually increments, which can be far harder to notice and debug than a loud traceback.

— 'What will this code print?' questions involving nested functions, global, and nonlocal are a genuinely common way interviewers test whether a candidate understands Python at a level beyond copy-pasted syntax.

items.strong: 🔧 It's a Prerequisite for Decorators and Closures
items.text: — You genuinely cannot understand how decorators work, or confidently write your own, without a solid grasp of enclosing scope and how nested functions capture outer variables.

items.strong: 🧠 It Reinforces a Precise, Useful Mental Model
items.text: — The LEGB search order is a genuinely reusable mental tool — once it's solid, reading unfamiliar code with nested functions and closures becomes dramatically less mysterious.

— Knowing when reaching for global is a code smell (heavy reliance on shared mutable global state) versus when it's a reasonable, deliberate choice (a small script's simple configuration) is a real design judgment call this understanding enables.

items.strong: 🇮🇳 It's a Standard Deep-Dive Topic Alongside Functions in Indian Curricula
items.text: — Scope, alongside *args/**kwargs and recursion, is typically given dedicated coverage in Indian engineering college Python courses and interview-prep material, precisely because it reveals genuine conceptual understanding.

sections.title: Namespaces vs Scope — A Distinction Worth Making Precisely

blocks.text: These two terms get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they describe genuinely different things, and being precise about the difference sharpens your understanding of both.

items.text: — is the actual mapping from names to objects — practically, a dictionary Python maintains behind the scenes, associating variable names with the objects they currently refer to. Every module, every function call, and every class has its own separate namespace.

— is the RULE for which namespaces are visible, and in what order, from a particular point in your code. Scope is what tells Python which namespace (or namespaces) to actually search when resolving a name.

— LEGB describes the specific sequence of namespaces — Local namespace, then Enclosing function's namespace, then Global (module) namespace, then Built-in namespace — that scope rules make visible and searchable, in that order, from any given line of code.

— locals() returns a dictionary of the current local namespace; globals() returns the current module's global namespace; these are genuinely useful for debugging exactly what names are visible and what values they currently hold at a specific point in your code.

rows: A concrete mapping of names to objects
A function's local variables, accessible via locals()

blocks.text: These come up regularly in Python interviews, particularly around closures, global state, and predicting output for nested-function code.

items.q: Q1. What is the LEGB rule in Python?
items.a: LEGB describes the exact order Python searches when resolving a variable name: Local scope (the current function's own namespace) first, then Enclosing scope (any outer function this one is nested inside), then Global scope (the current module's top-level namespace), then Built-in scope (Python's own reserved names like len or print). Python uses the first match it finds and stops searching.

items.q: Q2. Why does count += 1 inside a function raise UnboundLocalError even when count exists as a global variable?
items.a: Because Python determines, at compile time, that any name assigned anywhere within a function body is local to that entire function — and count += 1 counts as an assignment. This makes count local for the whole function, so when the right-hand side of += tries to READ count before any local value has been assigned to it, Python raises UnboundLocalError. The global variable with the same name is never actually reached.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between the global and nonlocal keywords?
items.a: global tells Python that a name inside a function refers to a variable at the module's top-level (global) scope, allowing that function to reassign it. nonlocal tells Python that a name inside a nested function refers to a variable in the nearest ENCLOSING function's scope (not the module-level global), allowing that nested function to reassign it. global reaches all the way to module level; nonlocal reaches only to the closest enclosing function.

items.q: Q4. Do if, for, and while blocks create their own scope in Python?
items.a: No. Unlike many other languages, Python's if, for, and while blocks do not create a new scope. A variable assigned inside one of these blocks remains accessible after the block ends, within the same enclosing function or module — scope in Python is determined by functions (and modules), not by arbitrary code blocks.

items.q: Q5. Do you need the global or nonlocal keyword to READ a variable from an outer scope inside a function?
items.a: No. Reading a variable from an enclosing or global scope requires no special keyword at all — Python's normal LEGB lookup handles that automatically. global and nonlocal are only required when you intend to REASSIGN that name inside the function; without the keyword, an assignment would instead create a new local variable rather than modifying the outer one.

items.q: Q6. What is a closure, and how does it relate to Python's Enclosing scope?
items.a: A closure occurs when a nested function references a variable from its enclosing function's scope, and that nested function is then used (often returned and called) after the enclosing function has already finished executing. The nested function 'closes over' and retains access to that enclosing variable, which is precisely what Python's Enclosing scope in the LEGB rule makes possible.

items.q: Q7. Why does calling append() on a list parameter inside a function not require the global or nonlocal keyword, even though it changes the list?
items.a: Because my_list.append(x) is not an assignment to the name my_list — it's a method call that mutates the object my_list already refers to, in place. Only reassigning the NAME itself (my_list = something_new) triggers Python's local-by-default rule and requires global/nonlocal to instead modify the outer variable. Mutating the object the name already points to needs neither keyword.

items.q: Q8. What does locals() and globals() return in Python, and how are they useful for debugging scope issues?
items.a: locals() returns a dictionary representing the current local namespace at the point it's called — every variable currently visible in the local scope, with its current value. globals() returns the equivalent dictionary for the current module's global namespace. Both are genuinely useful for debugging exactly which variables Python considers local versus global at a specific point in your code, especially when tracking down an unexpected UnboundLocalError.

blocks.text: Work through these before checking the answers. Correctly predicting when a scope error happens — not just what value gets printed — is the real test here.

items.q: 1. What is the output of: x = 'global' \n def show(): print(x) \n show()
items.a: global. Since x is only READ inside show(), never assigned, Python's LEGB search finds no local x, moves on to check Enclosing (none exists here), then finds x in Global scope and uses that value — no global keyword is needed for reading.

items.q: 2. What happens when you run: x = 'global' \n def show(): print(x); x = 'local' \n show()?
items.a: UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'x' where it is not associated with a value. Because x is assigned somewhere in show() (the line x = 'local'), Python treats x as local for the ENTIRE function — including the print(x) line that comes before the assignment, which now tries to read a local x that doesn't have a value yet.

items.q: 3. Trace this: for i in range(3): pass \n print(i) — what does it print, and why doesn't this raise an error?
items.a: 2. Since for loops don't create their own scope in Python, the loop variable i remains accessible after the loop ends, still holding its final value from the last completed iteration.

items.q:
4. What is the output of: def outer(): x = 'outer' 
 def inner(): x = 'inner'; print(x) 
 inner() 
 print(x) 
 outer()
items.a: inner, then outer. Inside inner(), x = 'inner' creates a genuinely separate local variable for inner() alone, printing 'inner'. Back in outer()'s own scope, its own x variable was never touched by inner() at all (no nonlocal was used), so it still holds 'outer'.

items.q: 5. What would change in the previous question if nonlocal x were added as the first line inside inner()?
items.a: It would print inner, then inner — both prints show 'inner'. With nonlocal x declared, the assignment x = 'inner' inside inner() now modifies outer()'s own x variable directly, rather than creating a separate local one, so when outer() later prints x, it sees the modified value.

items.q: 6. What is the output of: list = [1, 2, 3] \n print(list(range(3)))
items.a: TypeError: 'list' object is not callable. Assigning list = [1, 2, 3] creates a local (or global, depending on where this runs) variable that shadows Python's built-in list type within that scope. The subsequent call list(range(3)) now tries to CALL the list object [1, 2, 3] as if it were a function, which fails because lists aren't callable.

items.q: 7. What does make_multiplier(3) return, functionally, given: def make_multiplier(factor): def multiply(x): return x * factor \n return multiply — and what does make_multiplier(3)(10) evaluate to?
items.a: It returns the inner multiply function itself, which has closed over factor=3 from its enclosing scope. Calling make_multiplier(3)(10) immediately calls that returned function with x=10, computing 10 * 3, which evaluates to 30.

items.q: 8. Why does globals()['x'] = 'changed' work to modify a global variable x from inside a function, even without the global keyword?
items.a: globals() returns the actual dictionary Python uses to store the module's global namespace, not a copy — directly modifying an entry in that dictionary genuinely changes the global variable, bypassing the need for the global keyword entirely. This works because it isn't a normal name assignment at all; it's a dictionary mutation performed on the real underlying namespace object, similar in principle to why mutating a mutable argument doesn't require global/nonlocal either.

sections.title: Conclusion — LEGB Is the Quiet Rule Behind Almost Every 'Why Isn't This Updating' Bug

blocks.text: Scope is one of those Python topics that rarely gets its own dedicated attention early on, and then quietly turns out to be the actual explanation behind a real share of the confusing bugs beginners hit in their first few months. UnboundLocalError, a counter that never increments, a variable that seems to 'reset' unexpectedly inside a function — these almost always trace back to the same underlying mechanism: Python's local-by-default assignment rule, working exactly as designed, just not as the developer expected.

If you're a complete beginner, the priority is internalising the LEGB search order and the local-by-default assignment rule until predicting scope behaviour becomes automatic, not something you have to consciously reason through every time. If you're writing real, shared code, the priority shifts to judgment: recognising when reaching for global is a reasonable, deliberate choice versus when it's a sign that state should be passed explicitly as a function argument instead.

blocks.text: The habit worth carrying forward: whenever a function seems to be silently ignoring an update to a variable you expected it to change, the very first question to ask isn't 'is my logic wrong' — it's 'does this variable name get assigned anywhere inside this function, and did I mean for that to create a new local one.' That single question resolves an outsized share of Python's most confusing-looking bugs almost instantly.

Scope is a search order, not a mystery. Know the four letters, know exactly what triggers 'local,' and know precisely which keyword reaches outside it — everything else about reading and writing variable-heavy Python code gets noticeably clearer from there. 🐍

items.q: What is the LEGB rule in Python?
items.a: LEGB is the order Python follows when resolving a variable name: Local scope (the current function's own variables) first, then Enclosing scope (any outer function it's nested inside), then Global scope (the current module's top-level variables), then Built-in scope (Python's own reserved names like len and print). Python uses the first matching name it finds in that search order.

items.q: Why do I get UnboundLocalError when trying to modify a variable inside a Python function?
items.a: This happens when a variable is assigned somewhere inside a function (like count += 1) without first declaring it with global or nonlocal. Python decides at compile time that any assigned name is local to the whole function, so trying to read that name before its local assignment has actually run — as happens with += reading the current value first — raises UnboundLocalError, even if a variable with the same name exists at module level.

items.q: What is the difference between global and nonlocal in Python?
items.a: global lets a function modify a variable defined at the module's top level (global scope). nonlocal lets a nested function modify a variable defined in its nearest enclosing function's scope, rather than the module-level global or a new local variable. Use global for module-level state; use nonlocal for closures and nested-function patterns.

items.q: Do Python's if and for blocks create a new variable scope?
items.a: No. Unlike many other programming languages, Python's if, for, and while blocks do not create their own scope. A variable assigned inside one of these blocks remains fully accessible after the block ends, within the same enclosing function or at module level.

items.q: Do I need the global keyword just to read a global variable inside a function?
items.a: No. Reading a variable from global (or enclosing) scope inside a function works automatically through Python's normal LEGB lookup, with no special keyword required. global and nonlocal are only needed when you want to REASSIGN that variable's value from inside the function, not merely read its current value.

items.q: What is a closure in Python, and how is it related to scope?
items.a: A closure happens when a nested function references a variable from its enclosing function's scope, and continues to have access to that variable even after the enclosing function has finished running. This is made possible specifically by Python's Enclosing scope — the 'E' in the LEGB rule — which was added to the language in Python 2.1 and remains the mechanism behind decorators and factory functions today.
